UNUSUAL ELECTROMYOGRAPHIC FINDINGS IN
A PATIENT WITH PRESUMPTIVE HASHIMOTO’S
THYROIDITIS, STIFF-PERSON SYNDROME, AND
HERPES ZOSTER MYELORADICULITIS
James Ha, Fredric Gorin, Lin Zhang, Bjorn Oskarsson,
Ricardo Maselli (Sacramento, CA)
INTRODUCTION: A 59-year-old woman presented with
progressive gait difficulty, stiffness and spasms of the left
foot, and zoster lesions on the buttocks.
OBJECTIVE: To describe the unusual combination of
needle EMG findings in a case of concomitant Hashimotos
thyroiditis, stiff-person syndrome, and herpes zoster
myeloradiculitis.
METHODS: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid analysis,
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine, and EDX
studies were used in the evaluation of this patient.
RESULTS: The patient's physical examination was significant
for weakness of the left semitendinosus and gluteus muscles.
Deep tendon reflexes were 2+ at the knees and 1+ at the
ankles. The Babinski reflex was present on the right. The
sensory examination showed sensory modalities to be intact
in all extremities. The laboratory examination was significant
for thyroglobulin antibody >3000 IU/ml. GAD antibody
was >250 IU/ml; varicella-zoster polymerase chain reaction
(PCR) was negative; cerebrospinal fluid showed white blood
cell count 0, protein 31, glucose 54, and oligoclonal bands
negative; creatine kinase was 108. MRI of the cervical and
lumbar spine showed degenerative changes. A NCS of
the bilateral lower extremities was normal. Needle EMG
showed denervation changes in lumbar paraspinal muscles,
continuous muscle activity in the bilateral gastrocnemius
muscles, as well as myokymia and neuromyotonia in the left
abductor hallucis muscle.
SUMMARY/CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates
an unusual combination of multiple disorders with both
expected and unexpected needle EMG findings, including
denervation potentials consistent with radiculitis,
continuous muscle activity typically seen in stiff-person
syndrome, and other findings including myokymia and
neuromyotonia not typically seen in these disorders. The
findings illustrate the possibility of various needle EMG
abnormalities presenting in complex neuromuscular cases
with multiple coexistent disorders.
